description:
Earth's surface is constantly shifting and evolving. This futuristic art museum features data about Earth's surface changes as art pieces in motion, the data strokes "dancing" to their background music. 

I am Devyanshi, a 15-year-old, driven by a busy brain and an urge to build. I'm the kind of person who would wake up at 3 am to write down ideas. I saw the challenge as an opportunity to strengthen my Python skills and practice the new HTML and CSS skills I've been developing.
summary:
Earth’s Afterimage is a futuristic digital art gallery built from real NASA–ISRO NISAR radar measurements. Each hall holds one living artwork, drawn from numbers and set to its own music.

In Ice in Motion, 15 radar measurements of a patch of Jakobshavn Glacier in Greenland set how far the strokes sway, to a slow waltz. In The Burned Land, 13 measurements of radar change after the July 2026 Saumos wildfire in France set how strongly the strokes flicker, to a fierce flamenco rhythm.

The project answers “Dancing with the SARs” by showing how a radar satellite sees change: by comparing two passes over the same place, like two partners in a dance. Radar sees through clouds, smoke and darkness, so it can reveal places a camera cannot. Each hall comes with plain-language notes on how to read the piece, its limits and its sources.
details:
Earth’s Afterimage: a radar-data art gallery

Earth’s Afterimage is a futuristic digital art gallery. Each of its two halls holds one living artwork, drawn from real measurements by NISAR, a NASA–ISRO radar satellite. We wanted to do more than make the data accessible. We wanted visitors to remember it.

How it works
NISAR, a NASA–ISRO radar satellite, passes over the same place about every 12 days. Comparing two passes shows what changed in between, and that difference is one measurement.

Each hall turns a series of these measurements into an artwork. The bigger the measurement, the more the strokes move: in the glacier hall more of the canvas lights up, and in the fire hall more orange marks appear where the radar signal changed. Brighter, thicker strokes mean we are more sure of the measurement.

A visitor opens each hall with a small interaction, then presses play or drags a slider to travel through the measurements in time. The artwork responds step by step, and a line along the bottom shows all the measurements so the visitor can see where they are in the series. Where there is no data, the canvas goes dark.

The music is optional and carries no data. The beat, drift and glow are animation, and each hall’s notes say what is data and what is not.

Hall 1: Ice in Motion (a slow waltz)

  • Visitors drop a warm drop from a cup onto the ice, and the ice cracks open into the piece. The cup stands for everyday routines, like a morning coffee, that connect to a warming world.
  • 15 radar measurements of a 1.6 km patch of Jakobshavn Glacier, Greenland, from October 2025 to October 2026, set how far the strokes sway.
  • The waltz is slow because glacier melt is slow, but it adds up. Below the canvas, a panel notes that the Greenland ice sheet has lost more ice than it gained for the 30th year in a row (DMI Polar Portal, via Carbon Brief).
  • From 8 January to 25 June 2026 there is no data. The canvas goes dark, and we did not fill the gap.

Hall 2: The Burned Land (a fierce flamenco)

  • Visitors light a cigarette at a candle flame to open the piece. A lit cigarette is one common way fires start in France. Reports estimate smoking to account for 10–15% of forest fire starts in France (Imep-CNRS, via Sud Radio).
  • 13 radar measurements from May to October 2026 follow the July 2026 Saumos wildfire in France. A slider lets people compare the land from before the fires to after the fires, allowing users to compare and understand the change when the change is minimal(the first dots on the data line)
  • Before the fire, the piece stays still, because the radar shows no change yet. We kept that stillness as part of the piece.

Why it is creative
The challenge title, “Dancing with the SARs”, compared changing surfaces on Earth to a dance, so we gave each artwork the dance that suits it: a waltz for slow ice, flamenco for a fire that grows from a spark into flames that consume whole landscapes. The music is optional, original and carries no data. The openings turn each subject into something a visitor does. Even the pauses still flow with the animation and the music.

Made to be accessible and honest

  • Every hall has a plain-language “How to read this” guide and a “Read the data” section that says what the numbers do not mean.
  • Sound is off by default. There is a “Skip opening” button, a light and dark mode, and a visible focus outline for keyboard users.
  • The pieces are drawings made from numbers, not photographs or maps. The context panels come from press reports and are labelled as not NISAR measurements. The data come from NASA’s Beta and Provisional collections, which are not fully validated, and the page says so.

Benefits and impact
The gallery makes a hard-to-read dataset into a memorable experience for a general audience. It shows what radar can see through clouds, smoke and darkness, and it models honest science communication. We hope visitors leave curious about NISAR and about how everyday choices connect to glaciers and fires.

Tools
Python (asf_search, h5py, numpy, matplotlib) to download and process the data. The gallery is one HTML page with no libraries and no network calls. The music is generated in the browser with the Web Audio API. Claude wrote the app code and helped with sources and text. The idea, the data work and the design decisions are ours. The data exploration and the two small data files were prepared before the event; all app code and design were built during the event.
